title: Does God Change His Mind?
subtitle: Classical theism, open theism, and Molinism. Three accounts of how God's knowledge and human freedom fit together.
triageNote: That God is sovereign, that he knows his creation truly, and that prayer matters are affirmed by every view on this page. What divides faithful believers is how to hold three things together: God's knowledge, God's sovereignty, and the reality of human freedom and of prayer. Open theism's denial that God knows future free choices is the most contested view here, and a number of churches regard it as crossing a line, so the debate runs warm. But it is conducted between people who all worship the God of the Bible and all want to honor both his greatness and our responsibility. Hold God's perfection and trustworthiness tightly. Hold your model of how foreknowledge and freedom fit together with care, and know which of these views your own tradition has affirmed and which it has questioned.
question: The Bible says two things that are hard to hold at once. It says God knows the end from the beginning, declares what is to come before it happens, and has numbered your days before one of them began. And it says God responds: Abraham bargains with God and God yields, Moses intercedes and God relents, Hezekiah prays and God adds fifteen years to his life, Nineveh repents and God does not send the disaster he announced. So which is it. Did God always know exactly what would happen, including every free choice you will ever make, so that the relenting is only apparent, a way of speaking. Or does God genuinely respond, adjust, and even change course in real partnership with creatures whose choices are not yet settled. And underneath that lies the oldest knot in theology: if God already knows, infallibly, what you will choose tomorrow, in what sense is the choice yours, and could you do otherwise. Three serious answers have been worked out, each defended by careful believers, each trying to keep both God's greatness and our freedom without sacrificing either. None of them is comfortable. Each pays a price somewhere.
whyItMatters:
Pray about this and you will feel why it matters. When you ask God for something, what do you think is happening. If God has eternally and unchangeably known and ordained everything, then your prayer is not informing him or moving him, and you have to find a different account of why prayer is not pointless, an account the tradition does have but which you must actually hold. If instead God responds in time to what you ask, then prayer is a real conversation that genuinely affects the future, which is bracing but raises the question of how much God then leaves open and uncertain. Your model of foreknowledge is, in the end, your theology of prayer, and almost no one prays without having settled it one way or another, however unconsciously.

It also decides what you do with suffering and guidance. If every event, including the worst thing that ever happened to you, was eternally known and woven into God's plan, then there are no accidents, which is either the deepest comfort or the heaviest weight, depending on the hour. If instead the future is partly open and God works with genuinely free creatures in a world where things can truly go wrong against his wishes, then your tragedy may not have been scripted, which spares God the charge of authoring it but raises the question of how secure his promises about the end can be. People reach for different answers here not out of carelessness but because each answer comforts in one place and aches in another.

And it touches the character of God himself. Is God the one who, from outside time, holds all of history in a single eternal glance, sovereign over every detail, never learning, never surprised. Or is God the one who enters time with us, takes real risks, genuinely waits to see what his children will do, and responds with the freshness of a true relationship. These are different Gods to live with, and the texts pull in both directions, which is exactly why the church has produced more than one faithful answer and why you should understand all of them before you settle.

positions.name: Classical theism: exhaustive foreknowledge and unchanging counsel
positions.inOneLine: God knows all things, past, present, and future, including every free choice, in one timeless act, and his eternal counsel does not change, so the texts where God relents describe his unchanging character meeting changed people, not a God who learns or revises.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with the comfort, because this doctrine is comfort before it is philosophy. Your future is not a fog that God peers into anxiously. It is fully known to him, every day of it, every choice, every sorrow and every mercy, held in a single eternal act of knowledge. The God I worship does not wait to see what you will do. He has numbered your days, written them in his book before one of them came to be. When the worst thing in your life happened, it did not catch him off guard and force an improvised response. He saw it from before the foundation of the world and had already bent it toward your good and his glory. That is a hard saying in the hour of grief, and it is also the only thing that has ever held me up in that hour.

Now the philosophy, because you will ask how this fits with your freedom. God's knowing what you will choose does not make you choose it, any more than my watching you read this sentence makes you read it. Knowledge follows its object; it does not force it. God, who is not trapped inside time the way we are, sees all of history at once, the way you might see a whole parade from a hill while the marchers experience it one float at a time. Your tomorrow is future to you, but it is present to the God who inhabits eternity. So he knows your free choice infallibly, not because he forces it, but because he sees it, as surely as I know what you did yesterday without having forced that either. Boethius said this fifteen centuries ago and it has not been improved upon: God's foreknowledge does not impose necessity on things, because God does not foreknow as we know future things, he sees them in his eternal present.

What then of the relenting, the bargaining, the God who seems to change his mind. I take those with full seriousness as Scripture and with full seriousness as accommodation. When the Bible says God relented over Nineveh, it tells the truth in the only language we could bear: God's unchanging character meeting a changed people. He always pardons the penitent; that is who he eternally is. So when Nineveh repents, the unchanging God's settled mercy meets them, and from inside time it looks like God changed his mind, when in fact what changed was Nineveh. The threat itself was the appointed means of the repentance. Hezekiah's added years, Moses' intercession, your prayers tonight, all of these are real causes that God eternally ordained as the means by which he would accomplish his unchanging ends. Prayer is not pointless in this view; prayer is one of the ordained instruments by which God brings about what he has decreed. You are not informing God or moving an unwilling God. You are taking your appointed place in a plan that included your prayer from eternity. Paul Helm and Bruce Ware have laid this out with care, and I find it both the most coherent and the most steadying: a God who never learns, never panics, never improvises, because he has seen and ordained the whole of it in love.

positions.name: Open theism: the genuinely open future
positions.inOneLine: God knows everything that can be known, but the free choices of the future are not yet there to be known, so God knows the future as a realm of possibilities he sovereignly works within, genuinely responds to his creatures, and the texts where he relents mean exactly what they say.
positions.bestCase:
Hear me out, because I am usually caricatured before I am understood. I affirm that God is omniscient. God knows everything that can be known, perfectly, infallibly, exhaustively. My claim is not that God's knowledge is limited but that the future free choices of creatures are not yet realities to be known, the way a square circle is not a thing God's omnipotence fails to make. If the future is partly open, partly composed of choices not yet made, then to know it as already settled would be to know falsely, and God never knows falsely. He knows the open future as open: all the possibilities, the probabilities, his own unshakable purposes, and the exhaustive present and past. What he does not foreknow as already fixed is what genuinely free creatures have not yet decided, because there is, as yet, no fact there to know.

Why do I hold this. First, because of freedom. I cannot make sense of a choice that is genuinely mine, genuinely able to go either way, if it was infallibly known and therefore certain a billion years before I was born. If God knew with certainty yesterday that I would sin tomorrow, then it was certain yesterday, and certainty about my act before I exist is, to me, indistinguishable from its being settled without me. The classical answers have never quieted that for me. Second, and far more important, because of the Bible. Read the narrative plainly and you meet a God who tests Abraham and then says, now I know that you fear God, as if he learned something. A God who says of Israel's atrocities, it did not enter my mind that they should do this thing. A God who grieves that he made man, who relents over Nineveh, who hangs the future of a city on whether it repents and means it. Greg Boyd and John Sanders have shown how pervasive this language is, not a few odd verses but the texture of the whole story, and I think the burden is on those who turn every one of these into a figure of speech to ask whether they are reading the Bible or reading a philosophy back into it.

What do I gain. A God of genuine relationship. When I pray, I am not reciting lines in a script written before time; I am speaking to a God who truly hears and whose response is truly responsive, who has chosen to make the future partly depend on the prayers and choices of his children. When tragedy strikes, I do not have to say God ordained the murder of a child from eternity for a hidden good purpose; I can say the world has real freedom, that things can genuinely go against God's wishes, that God did not script the horror and is now at work to redeem it. And I lose nothing of his greatness, because it takes a greater God, not a lesser one, to set out toward a real goal through a world of free creatures and unfailingly reach it, the way a master can win the game without controlling every move his opponent makes. The God who needs to fix everything in advance is, to me, less sovereign, not more, than the God who can rule a genuinely open world and still bring it home.
advocates: Gregory A. Boyd (God of the Possible)

positions.name: Molinism: middle knowledge
positions.inOneLine: God knows not only everything that will happen and everything that could happen, but also what every free creature would freely do in any possible circumstance, and by this middle knowledge he sovereignly orders a world of genuinely free people without forcing a single choice.
positions.bestCase:
I want to give you both things, exhaustive foreknowledge and libertarian freedom, and I think there is a way to have them, which is why I find this view the most satisfying of the three. It turns on a kind of divine knowledge the other views overlook, what Luis de Molina, the sixteenth-century Jesuit, called middle knowledge, scientia media. Let me build it in three steps, the way Molina did.

First, God has natural knowledge: he knows all necessary truths and everything that could possibly happen, every way any world could go. This knowledge is prior to any decision of his will. Third, after he decides what to create, God has free knowledge: he knows everything that will actually happen in the world he chose. So far this is standard. The genius is the step in between, the middle knowledge, which is why it is called middle. Before deciding what to create, God knows not just what could happen but what every possible free creature would freely do in every possible situation it might be placed in. He knows that if you were placed in exactly these circumstances, with this history and these influences, you would freely choose this. Not that he forces it. That you would freely do it. These are the counterfactuals of creaturely freedom, and Scripture seems to assume God has them: Jesus says that if the miracles done in Capernaum had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. That is a truth about what free people would have freely done in circumstances that never happened. God knew it.

Now watch what this lets God do. Knowing, by middle knowledge, exactly how every possible person would freely act in every possible setting, God surveys the infinite range of possible worlds he could create, and he sovereignly chooses to actualize the one world whose entire history, freely enacted by its creatures, accomplishes his purposes. He does not push a single choice. Every choice is genuinely free, could have gone otherwise. And yet the whole sweep of history unfolds exactly as God intended, because he selected this world knowing precisely how its free creatures would freely fill it. This is how I can say both sentences without crossing my fingers: you are truly free, able to do otherwise, and God's providence is meticulous and his foreknowledge exhaustive. The relenting texts I read as God's sincere expression within the very world he chose, the conditional warnings that are themselves the ordained means; God knew Nineveh would repent if Jonah preached, and that is why Jonah was sent. William Lane Craig has argued that middle knowledge dissolves more theological puzzles than any other single idea, and whether or not it does all he claims, I find it the one account that refuses to buy God's sovereignty by shrinking my freedom, or my freedom by shrinking God's knowledge. It pays its price elsewhere, in the metaphysics of those counterfactuals, and I think that price is worth paying.

biblicalEvidence.summary: I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, my counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose. God declares the future and guarantees that his purpose will be done.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for open theism's strongest form, since God declares specific things not yet done and stakes his uniqueness on accomplishing his whole purpose in advance.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism takes this as exhaustive foreknowledge and unchanging decree. Molinism agrees God knows and secures the end, by middle knowledge of how free creatures will act. Open theism reads it as God's certainty about his own purposes and the things he himself will bring about, which he can declare without claiming to foreknow every free human choice, since God can guarantee his ends through his own action.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them. The psalmist's days are written in God's book before any of them exist.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for open theism, since the days of a life appear already written before they are lived, which sounds like settled foreknowledge.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism and Molinism both read this as God's knowledge of a whole life in advance. Open theism reads the language as the poetry of God's intimate care and purpose for a life, his loving intention and providence over the psalmist, rather than a technical claim that every future free act is already fixed, noting the psalm's register is praise, not metaphysics.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Do not lay your hand on the boy, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son from me. After the testing of Abraham, God says now I know, as though the test yielded knowledge.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for exhaustive foreknowledge in its strongest form, since God says now I know after the event, suggesting the testing produced something God then knew.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Open theism reads now I know as God genuinely coming to know Abraham's proven faithfulness through the free act of obedience. Classical theism reads it as God bringing to light, in time and for Abraham's sake and ours, a faith God eternally knew, the now I know marking the demonstration, not a gain in divine knowledge. Molinism agrees God eternally knew what Abraham would do and the test actualizes it in history.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Open theism, with classical theism reading it as principle
biblicalEvidence.summary: God relented of the disaster he had said he would do to Nineveh. Jeremiah states it as a principle: if a nation I threatened turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster I intended. God's responses to nations are conditional on their response.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a rigid view of unchanging decree taken to mean God never genuinely responds, since the relenting is tied directly to the people's repentance and stated as a general principle.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Open theism reads this as God's genuine, contingent response within a real relationship: the future of Nineveh truly hung on its repentance. Classical theism reads it as the unchanging God's consistent character, he always relents toward the penitent, so the principle describes God's steadfastness, not his changeability, and the threat was the ordained means of repentance. Molinism reads God as knowing by middle knowledge that Nineveh would repent if warned, and sending the warning for that reason.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Woe to you, Chorazin, says Jesus, for if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Jesus states what people in cities that never saw the miracles would have freely done.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for open theism, since Jesus asserts a definite truth about what free creatures would have done in circumstances that never occurred, the very counterfactuals open theism says are not there to be known.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Molinism takes this as direct evidence of middle knowledge: God knows what free creatures would do in unrealized circumstances. Classical theism reads it as God's knowledge of all possibilities and as a vivid statement of Chorazin's greater guilt, without committing to a distinct middle knowledge. Open theism reads it as God's knowledge of probabilities and character, what those cities would likely have done, rather than a settled counterfactual of libertarian freedom.

biblicalEvidence.summary: David asks the Lord whether the men of Keilah will hand him over to Saul if he stays, and whether Saul will come down. God answers that they will, and that Saul will. David then leaves, and neither thing happens, because David acted on the answer.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a simple view that God only knows what will actually happen, since God answers what would happen under conditions that, because of the answer, never come to pass.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Molinism treats this as a showcase of middle knowledge: God knows what Saul and the men of Keilah would freely do if David stayed, even though David's leaving means they never do it. Classical theism reads it as God's knowledge of conditional outcomes within his comprehensive knowledge. Open theism reads the answers as God's declaration of what would result given present dispositions and intentions, which David's free action then changes.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Classical theism, with Molinism affirming it
biblicalEvidence.summary: This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. The crucifixion is both the foreordained plan of God and the free, guilty act of those who carried it out.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for open theism's strongest form, since the central event of history is said to be both definitely planned and foreknown by God and freely, culpably done by men.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism reads this as the paradigm: God's sovereign plan and human free agency in the same event, the plan including the free acts. Molinism reads it as God ordaining the cross through his middle knowledge of how Judas, Pilate, and the crowd would freely act. Open theism reads God's plan as his settled purpose to redeem through a rejected Messiah, with the certainty resting on God's resolve and the entrenched dispositions of the actors rather than on a foreknown script of each free choice.

biblicalEvidence.summary: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. God works all things according to the counsel of his will.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that makes large stretches of history fall outside God's purposeful working, since Paul says God works all things according to his counsel.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism reads all things as comprehensive, God's sovereign counsel embracing everything. Molinism agrees, locating the how in middle knowledge, God arranging all things by choosing this world. Open theism reads works all things as God working in and through all things toward his ends, sovereignly and unfailingly, without requiring that every detail was eternally fixed, since God can work all things toward his purpose in a partly open world.

weighing:
My judgment, offered tentatively, because this is one of the places where I most distrust anyone, including myself, who sounds too sure.

I find myself unable to follow open theism to its conclusion, and I want to say why with respect, because its defenders have read the narrative more honestly than their critics often admit. The relenting texts are not a handful of oddities; they are the texture of the story, and open theism takes them seriously where classical theism sometimes rushes past them. But when I reach the texts where God declares specific future free acts, Peter's denials named before the rooster, the cross planned before it happened, the end declared from the beginning, I cannot square them with a future genuinely unknown to God in its free details. And the cross decides it for me. If the central act of redemption was not certainly foreknown, then the gospel itself was a gamble, and I cannot build my hope on a God who was hoping it would work out.

Between classical theism and Molinism, I lean, gently, toward holding the comprehensiveness of classical theism while finding Molinism's middle knowledge a genuinely useful tool for one thing the bare classical view leaves murky: how God can ordain a world without authoring sin and without crushing real freedom. The Capernaum and Keilah passages do seem to show God knowing what free creatures would do in circumstances that never occurred, and that is exactly what middle knowledge names. So if you pressed me, I would say I want classical theism's exhaustive foreknowledge and unchanging counsel, the comfort that your days are written and your worst hour was not a surprise, and I am glad to borrow Molinism's middle knowledge to explain how that sovereignty can run through genuinely free choices rather than over them. The price Molinism pays, the strange metaphysics of those counterfactuals, what grounds them, troubles me, and I hold the whole thing loosely.

What I will not do is pretend the relenting texts cost me nothing. They do. The honest position keeps feeling the pull of the God who responds, who waits, who is moved, even while confessing the God who knows the end from the beginning. I would rather live inside that tension than resolve it too cheaply in either direction. Your days are known and your prayers are real, and exactly how both are true at once is something I expect to understand better on the other side than I do now.
charitableDisagreement:
This debate runs warmer than most, so a few words of restraint. Open theism is the most contested view here, and a number of faithful churches and theologians regard its denial of exhaustive foreknowledge as a serious error, some as outside the bounds. If you share that judgment, you may say so honestly, but say it knowing that men like Greg Boyd and John Sanders are not playing games with the Bible; they are wrestling with texts that the rest of us are often too quick to explain away, and they hold their view to protect God's goodness and the reality of relationship, which are precious things. Do not pretend their motives are careless. And if you are drawn to open theism, understand why so many resist it: not because they love a cold determinism, but because they fear that a God who does not certainly know the future cannot certainly keep his promises, and the cross with it.

Between classical theism and Molinism the temperature is lower, and rightly so. These are two ways of holding the same convictions, exhaustive foreknowledge and a sovereign God, with a real disagreement about the machinery underneath. Argue the machinery freely; do not make a wall of it.

So, is it a hill to die on. God's perfection, his trustworthiness, his sovereign goodness, and the genuine reality of prayer, yes, those are not negotiable. But the precise model of how foreknowledge and freedom fit together is a second-order question on which serious believers have differed for centuries, even granting that one of the views here sits closer to the boundary than the others. Confess the God who is great and good and keeps his word. Hold your theory of how he knows tomorrow with the humility of someone who has not yet seen tomorrow himself.

relatedDebates.note: How God's sovereignty relates to human choice runs straight into the question of salvation: whether God's electing grace is the decisive cause of faith, or whether it cooperates with a free human response. The Calvinist, Arminian, and other accounts of grace and the will sit right next to this debate, and your view of foreknowledge often tracks your view of election.

relatedDebates.topic: Does God suffer and is God moved?
relatedDebates.note: The texts where God relents sit close to the texts where God grieves. Whether God genuinely responds to and is affected by his creatures is the impassibility question, and how you read God changing his mind is connected to how you read God being moved. The impassibility page takes up that nearby debate.

relatedDebates.topic: Immutability and the unchanging counsel of God
relatedDebates.note: Behind the question of whether God changes his mind stands the doctrine that God does not change. How strongly you hold immutability shapes how you read every relenting text, and whether divine responsiveness is real change or the unchanging God meeting changed creatures. The attributes page maps that prior question.
